modal-content.p: Dependent care benefits are provided by an employer and used to care for dependents, such as young children and family members with disabilities.
Dependent care benefits can include:

ol.li: Pre-tax contributions you made under a dependent care flexible spending arrangement (FSA)
Amounts your employer paid directly to either you or your care provider for the care of a qualifying person while you work or look for work
The fair market value of care in a daycare facility provided or sponsored by your employer

modal-content.p: When you get dependent care benefits from your employer, they’re tax-free. But, in some cases you may need to pay taxes on these benefits later when you file your taxes.

div.h2: In , did you have a household employee who came to your home to provide child or dependent care?
div.p: We ask this because if you had a household employee, you may need to pay employment taxes and file Schedule H (Form 1040) with your federal tax return. Direct File doesn’t yet support this.
They may be a household employee if:

ul.li: They come to your home and you control what work is done and how it’s done
You hired them and pay them directly (even if they were recommended by an agency)
You have an Employer Identification Number (EIN) and provided them with a Form W-2

div.p: They may not be a household employee if:

ul.li: They provide the care from their own home or place of business
You pay an agency to place them in your home and the agency controls what work is done and how it’s done

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What does it mean to forfeit or carry forward dependent care benefits?

modal-content.p: If you had an employer-provided dependent care plan, your employer set aside an amount to cover your dependent care expenses.

A forfeited amount is any amount that your employer set aside, but that you didn’t use on qualified dependent care expenses in . Forfeited amounts don’t include amounts you expect to receive in the future.
An amount that was carried forward includes unused dependent care benefits from that your employer allowed you to carry forward and use during the grace period in , which ends on March 15, .

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What are qualified dependent care expenses?

modal-content.p: Qualified expenses include amounts paid for the care of a qualifying person while you (or your spouse if you’re filing jointly) worked or looked for work. The main purpose of the care must be for the qualifying person’s well-being and protection.
Qualified expenses must be paid to a qualified care provider. According to the IRS, a qualified care provider cannot be:

ul.li: Your dependent
Your spouse (at any time in )
The parent of your qualifying child
Your biological child, adopted child, stepchild, or foster child unless they were age 19 or older by the end of

modal-content.p: Some expenses that may qualify:

ul.li: Household services that are at least partly for the care of a qualifying person and that are needed to run a home, like the services of a cook, maid, babysitter, housekeeper, or cleaning person
Expenses for a child in nursery school, preschool, or similar programs for children below kindergarten level
Expenses for before- or after-school care of a child in kindergarten or a higher grade
Expenses for day camp
Expenses for a dependent care center that complies with state and local regulations
Fees paid to an agency to get care provider services
Deposits and application fees paid to an agency or preschool (as long as they weren’t forfeited)

modal-content.p: Some expenses that don’t qualify:

ul.li: Expenses to attend kindergarten or a higher grade
Summer school and tutoring programs
Overnight camps
Expenses for food, lodging, clothing, education, entertainment, unless they were related to the care of the qualifying person and can’t be separated from the total cost
Child support payments

modal-content.p: This is not a complete list. Refer to Publication 503 to learn more about which expenses qualify.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: How does including combat pay affect your taxable dependent care benefits?

modal-content.p: Including combat pay in your earned income can help reduce the amount of your dependent care benefits that are taxed.

If you decide to include combat pay in your earned income, this will only be used to calculate how much of your dependent care benefits are taxed. It can only be helpful, and will never lead to more of your benefits being taxed.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Which tax situations may lower the amount of taxable dependent care benefits?

modal-content.p: To figure how much of your dependent care benefits are taxable, the IRS allows one or both taxpayers to be treated as having earned income for any month that they are:

ul.li: Full-time students
Physically or mentally unable to care for themselves

modal-content.p: For every month that they’re a full-time student or unable to care for themselves, they can be treated as having up to $250 in earned income if they have one qualifying person, and up to $500 in earned income if they have two or more qualifying people. This could mean that less of their benefits will be taxed.

p.a: Learn more about the rule for student-spouse or spouse not able to care for self.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Why can’t I change the country?

modal-content.p: Currently, Direct File only supports mailing written communications and refunds from the IRS to addresses in the United States.
If you must use an address outside the U.S., you’ll need to file using another product. Learn more about your filing options.
An Employer Identification Number (EIN) is also known as a federal tax identification number, and is used to identify a business entity.
EINs are 9-digit numbers.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What’s a Social Security number (SSN) or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN)?

modal-content.p: A Social Security number (SSN) is a unique identifier issued by the Social Security Administration.
An Individual Tax Identification Number (ITIN) is a type of tax ID number issued by the IRS.
SSNs and ITINs are 9-digit numbers.
